sections.overview: The Seychelles fruit bat, called sousouri locally, is the largest bat of the Seychelles and one of the archipelago’s two native mammals. It is a flying fox that feeds on fruit and flowers and is found across the central granitic islands.
sections.identification: A large fruit bat with dark brown fur, black wings and a bright orange-yellow head and neck, and a prominent snout. It weighs up to about 600 g, with a wingspan of up to 1.2 m according to one source and up to 1.5 m according to another.
sections.habitat: It occurs widely on the central granitic islands of the Seychelles, such as Mahé, Praslin and Cousine, and roosts in treetops. It can fly between neighbouring islands, for example between Praslin and Cousin. The Mammal Diversity Database now restricts the species to the Seychelles, treating the Comoros population as a separate species.
sections.diet: It eats fruit, nectar and pollen, including cultivated mangoes and papayas, and relies on a keen sense of smell and good eyesight to find food. It feeds noisily in fruiting trees, sometimes all night.
sections.behavior: Colonies roost together in treetops during the heat of the day, hanging by one foot, and the bats fly out in the late afternoon to feed. They are most often seen at dusk and dawn, and in greater numbers from November to February, when food is more plentiful, according to a Cousine Island account. On very calm days a few skim the sea and dip their chests in the water, for reasons not fully understood.
sections.reproduction: The sources consulted give no breeding season, litter size or age at maturity. The Seychelles Ministry of Environment announced a study to document the species’ feeding and breeding patterns, which suggests these remain poorly documented.
sections.ecology: As a pollinator and seed disperser, it helps native plants regenerate and is an important part of island ecosystems. A Seychelles environmentalist has noted that it disperses seeds of endemic plants.
sections.conservation: The Mammal Diversity Database lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. A 2004 report estimated about 8,500 bats in the Seychelles, and no newer count had been made by the time of a recent news article. It is hunted for a curry considered a delicacy, though no law forbids this, and it also suffers collisions with infrastructure and has been linked to power outages on Mahé.
